title: Planning ahead to boost activities
body: Gary Hunt reported for the Herald that the Associated Student Government was planning ahead to boost campus activities. The article ran in the second week of William Menser's year as the government's first student regent.
note: The article is verified ("Hunt, Gary. Associated Student Government Planning Ahead to Boost Activities"). But Menser was the Associated Students president, elected in the landslide reported in 46:20, not a student regent. Herald 47:10 (2 Nov 1967) still runs "Henry Ward Favors Student on Board of Regents," i.e. the student-regent seat was an open campaign question at the time, not a post Menser held.

title: The Association opens the Associated Students year
body: The Herald announced that a concert by the Association would open the Associated Students entertainment year. Photographs of the concert ran in the issue of 24 October.
note: 48:4 has "'Association' Concert Billed to Open Associated Students Year" — a billing, not a held concert, and it gives no date. The entry files it as a concert on 10 October, which is only the issue date. The 24 October photographs are in an issue that is not cited.

title: Lyne's account: entertainment becomes a cultural programme
body: In his signed statement in the 1971 Talisman, president John Lyne wrote that the entertainment side of the government's work had been expanded into a cultural programmes concept, that big-name concerts continued but names outside the top forty such as Ravi Shankar had been brought in, and that theatrical events had been sponsored including the co-sponsorship of "1776." He also recorded that a student-run lecture series had been added that year, that the student discount programme with local merchants had been maintained, and that the government was working towards a legal service for students including a legal defence fund and a student advocates' corps.
note: The 1971 Talisman contains no signed statement by Lyne. The Lyne material is an interview profile running roughly pp. 80-85, not p. 66, and it does not contain the listed content. Repeated full-text searches show the volume has no instance of "discount," "legal," "advocate," "forty," or "cultural programs." Only unattributed captions for Ravi Shankar and "1776" exist, and the lecture series is named as "The University Lecture Series," not a student-run one.

title: The year's programme summed up in the yearbook
body: The 1972 Talisman summarised Linda Jones's year under the heading "A.S. makes great strides in implementing new programs": in entertainment, mini-concerts, a coffee house in West Hall and the Gaslight film series joined several top-name musical groups and lecturers. It also recorded that the Associated Students conducted the elections for class officers, Who's Who and Homecoming queen, held the October mock election for governor, ran a symposium at which students could question administrators, sponsored the Homecoming dance, and revived the Kentucky Student Association among the state's student governments.
note: The heading "A.S. makes great strides in implementing new programs" does not appear in the 1972 Talisman, nor do "Gaslight," "Cellar," "West Hall" or "coffee house." The volume does mention Who's Who, a Homecoming queen and a Kentucky Student Association convention, but in unrelated passages, not as an itemised summary of what Associated Students ran. The p. 272 summary as described is not in the source.

title: Sam Ervin analyses Watergate
body: Senator Sam Ervin, chairman of the Senate Watergate committee, spoke at Western on 2 April 1974 under the contract ASG had signed in February. The Talisman recorded that the 1973-74 lecture series ended with Ervin and with Representative John Conyers of Michigan, a member of the House Judiciary Committee who voted for impeachment.
note: Herald 53:50, 5 Apr 1974 does report the event ("Caudill, Tom. Sam Ervin Analyzes Watergate Situation"), and 53:48 has "Sam Ervin to Speak Tuesday" (Tuesday = 2 Apr). But nothing ties Ervin to ASG: the 1974 Talisman lists him only under "Other lecturers scheduled for 1974", alongside Vincent Price, in a passage about the University Lecture Series. The "contract ASG had signed in February" is unsupported. The claim that the Talisman recorded the series ending with Ervin and Rep. John Conyers is contradicted - Conyers does not appear anywhere in the 1974 Talisman (the only Conyers in its index is a student, Mary Anne Conyers); Conyers spoke, per Herald 29 Mar 1974, but with no ASG or series attribution.

title: Charles Berlitz opens the ASG lecture series on the Bermuda Triangle
body: Charles Berlitz, author of 'The Bermuda Triangle', opened the ASG lecture series in Van Meter on 9 September 1975 to a standing-room-only audience. He told them that since 1945 more than 100 planes and ships and 1,000 people had vanished in the region, and ran through theories from magnetisation to alien beings.
note: The cited Herald 51:4, 9 Sep 1975 carries "Hoodoo Sea to Be Subject of Associated Student Government Lecture - Charles Berlitz, Bermuda Triangle" - a same-day advance notice ('to be subject of'), which cannot report a standing-room-only audience or the content. All of it is in the uncited 1976 Talisman: "shadows lent an eerie atmosphere to the standing-room-only audience... Charles Berlitz... opened the Associated Student Government (ASG) lecture series... In the Sept. 9 lecture... Since 1945, more than 100 planes and ships and 1,000 people have vanished", with the magnetisation and alien-beings theories.

title: Harrison Salisbury lectures
body: The Pulitzer Prize-winning newspaper columnist Harrison Salisbury lectured on the evening of 30 March 1976. He was one of the spring speakers scheduled by ASG's lecture committee.
note: The cited Herald 51:50, 30 Mar 1976 carries "Journalist to Lecture Tonight - Harrison Salisbury" - a same-day advance notice. The 1976 Talisman likewise only says he was among "Other lecturers scheduled in the spring... Harrison Salisbury on March 30 and author Truman Capote on April 21." Nothing I could reach reports that the lecture actually took place.

title: Dick Gregory draws about 400
body: Civil rights activist Dick Gregory gave a free afternoon lecture in the Center Theater as part of the Black Awareness Symposium, opening with comic lines before turning on United States actions in Vietnam, the Middle East, Iran and Jonestown. About 400 came, against 36 for the Reverend Arthur Langford's "Martin Luther King Jr.: A Portrait" in February. That evening the Heritage Hall Jazz Band from New Orleans played to a half-filled Van Meter Auditorium.
note: The facts all check out but the source never ties the event to student government. Talisman 1979 pp.38-39 confirms: free afternoon lecture by Gregory in Center Theater; comic opening then criticism of US actions in 'Vietnam, the Middle East, Iran and Jonestown, Guyana'; Nemeth quoted 'The King portrayal drew only 36 people, but about 400 people showed up to hear Dick Gregory'; Langford's 'Martin Luther King Jr.: A Portrait' on Feb. 14 attracted 36; Heritage Hall Jazz Band from New Orleans in a half-filled Van Meter on March 22. But the Black Awareness Symposium section attributes the programme entirely to Tim Nemeth and the university, and the Talisman's own University Center Board section (p.82) lists 'Martin Luther King Jr.: A Portrait' and 'the Heritage Hall Jazz Band' as CENTER BOARD lectures-and-concerts programmes, not ASG ones. If you want the ASG tie for Gregory, it is in the 18 January 1979 Herald ('ASG signs 3 lectures'), which should be cited alongside. Two smaller points: the source does not say the jazz band played 'that evening', only that Gregory spoke 'earlier that day'; and it dates Langford to Feb. 14, which your 'in February' covers.

title: ASG's International Week
body: ASG ran International Week nightly in the university center in November 1980, with two or three countries featured each evening through films, lectures, folk dances and slides given by students and faculty from those countries. Programme chairman Osama Shariff opened the week with a talk on Palestine and a Red Cross film on Palestinian children, and the week closed on a presentation of Brazil and Colombia. Nine countries were covered in all: Switzerland, Palestine, Iceland, Malaysia, Colombia, Brazil, India, Pakistan and France.

src.label: College Heights Herald, Vol. 56, No. 22, 13 November 1980

note: The cited Herald supports the sponsorship and the opening night but not the two most specific claims. Herald 11-13-1980, Vol. 56 No. 22, 'ASG sponsors international affair': International Week 'sponsored by Associated Student Government'; 'The nightly event, which began Monday, ends with a final presentation on Brazil and Colombia at 7 tonight'; two or three countries each night using 'films, lectures, folk dances and slides'; students and faculty from those countries presenting; 'Program chairman Osama Shariff opened the activities Monday,' gave a talk on Palestine and showed 'a Red Cross film on how Palestinian children survive.' NOT in this issue: the nine-country list (Switzerland, Iceland, Malaysia, India, Pakistan, France are never named - I searched the full issue text) and the university-center venue. Both of those come from Talisman 1981 ('A year of resolutions'), which says 'Osama Sharif... coordinated the nightly programs in the university center. Nine countries - Switzerland, Palestine, Iceland, Malaysia, Colombia, Brazil, India, Pakistan and France - were featured.' Add that second citation and the entry stands.

title: Mock presidential election with the College Republicans
body: ASG co-sponsored a mock presidential election with the College Republicans on Tuesday 25 October, from 10:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. in the university center, with student identification cards required to vote. Public relations vice president Amos Gott said the aim was to see how Western felt as a community compared with Bowling Green and the national responses to the candidates, and expected a turnout at least as large as a student government election because everybody knew the candidates. Results were posted the next day on the glassed-in student government bulletin board in the university center.
note: REJECT - announcement written up as a completed event. Herald 64:17, 20 Oct 1988 is headlined "Mock election SCHEDULED; ASG hotline established" and reads "Associated Student Government is co-sponsoring a mock election with the College Republicans TUESDAY from 10:30 a.m. to 3 p.m. in the university center" - a Thursday paper describing the following Tuesday. The results line is future tense too: "The results WILL BE POSTED Wednesday in the glassed-in student government bulletin board in the university center, Gott said." The source therefore does not establish that the election happened, that anyone voted, or what the turnout was. The co-sponsorship, the times, the ID requirement, Amos Gott's stated purpose and his turnout expectation all match; only the tense and the dating are wrong.

title: Weekend in the Woods runs again on 23 and 24 October
body: President Donald Smith told congress on 12 October 1993 that Weekend in the Woods would be held on 23 and 24 October. The leadership retreat, which ASG had been running since the early 1980s, was still on the organisation's calendar a decade after the fourth annual weekend recorded in the 1987 Talisman.
note: REJECT as dated - the source records only the announcement. SGA minutes, 12 Oct 1993: President Donald Smith "also informed member of Weekend in the Woods on October 23-24." That single line is all there is. The minutes do not show the retreat took place, who went, where, or what it cost, so an entry dated 1993-10-23 with a title asserting it "runs again" overstates the record. The body text is honest about this, so the fix is small: redate to the 12 Oct meeting and retitle as an announcement, or cite the minutes of a later meeting. Also note the added claim that ASG "had been running [it] since the early 1980s" is an inference from the 1987 Talisman's "fourth annual," not something either source states.

title: SGA circulates flyers for a Jesse Jackson Jr. speech
body: Administrative vice president Scott Sivley passed out flyers at the 29 March 1994 congress meeting for Jesse Jackson Jr.'s speech on 18 April. The minutes record SGA distributing the publicity rather than booking the speaker, and name no fee or venue.
note: REJECT for an archive of events student government staged. SGA minutes, 29 Mar 1994, contain exactly one line: Administrative Vice-President Sivley "passed out flyers for Jesse Jackson, Jr.'s speech on April 18." That ties SGA to distributing publicity on 29 March and to nothing else - not to booking, funding, hosting or even attending, and the source gives no venue, sponsor or fee. It also does not establish that the 18 April speech occurred. The entry is commendably honest about all of this in its own body, which is why I would file it as a note against the 29 March meeting rather than as an SGA-staged speaker event dated 1994-04-18.

title: Designated driver cards go out to students
body: The designated driver cards SGA funded with $900 in November 1997 were distributed the day after this Herald report. The card entitled a designated driver to free soft drinks at participating restaurants instead of alcohol.

src.label: Herald 73:33, 17 Feb 1998 - Felkins, "Student Government Association's Designated Driver Cards Will Be Distributed Tomorrow"

note: Two independent problems. First, the money: the source is a Herald contents record whose only relevant line is 'Felkins, Melissa. Student Government Association's Designated Driver Cards Will Be Distributed Tomorrow - Drunk Driving, Alcohol'. It gives no $900 figure, nothing about November 1997 funding, and nothing about free soft drinks at participating restaurants. Second, the headline is an announcement of a future distribution, which the entry converts into a completed event. Issue is Vol. 73, No. 36, not 73:33.

title: The spring banquet and the senior banquet
body: SGA's spring banquet was held on Tuesday 27 April 2004 from 5 to 8 p.m. in the Kentucky Building, in place of the usual Congress meeting. The senior banquet followed the next evening from 7.30 to 9 p.m. in the same building, business attire required.

src.label: WKU SGA news page, 20 Apr 2004 (Wayback capture)

note: The source is prospective, and it also conflicts with SGA's own calendar on the time. The cited 20 April 2004 news item reads: 'The Spring Banquet will be at the regular Congress meeting time, except it will be in the Kentucky Building. It is currently scheduled from 5:00 - 8:00 pm. The Senior Banquet will be next Wednesday from 7:30 - 9:00 pm in the Kentucky Building. Please dress in business attire.' Venue, hours, business attire and the day-after sequence all match, and the dates work out to 27 and 28 April - but 'currently scheduled' is an announcement, which the entry reports as an event that was held. Separately, SGA's own Events Calendar lists the 27 April banquet at 6:00 PM, not 5 to 8.

title: Hidden Hacks of the Hill showed students what they were missing
body: WKU hosted Hidden Hacks of the Hill on 14 November 2017 in Downing Student Union, an SGA-funded event aimed at helping minority student groups find campus resources. The Writing Center, the Counseling and Testing Center and the WKU Food Pantry all tabled. Senator Divya Gangavelli spoke on the practical hacks, including how the White, Red and Purple bus lines could be used to get around campus and up the Hill.

src.label: Herald, 16 Nov 2017 - "Students learn the hidden hacks of the Hill"

note: The cited 16 Nov 2017 article credits the host as the university, not student government: 'WKU hosted Hidden Hacks of the Hill Tuesday, an event dedicated to helping minority student groups on campus familiarize themselves with on-campus resources.' It never says SGA funded or organised it - the sole SGA connection is that 'Student Government Association senator Divya Gangavelli took time to speak.' The words 'fund', 'bill' and '$200' do not appear. This is the pattern of a campus event not tied to SGA by the source. The funding claim is supported instead by the 1 Nov 2017 Herald piece, which reports Bill 20-17-F approving $200 for 'Hidden Hacks on the Hill' on 14 Nov. Everything else in the entry (Writing Center, Counseling and Testing Center, WKU Food Pantry tabling; Gangavelli on the White, Red and Purple lines and the Grise Hall route up the Hill) is accurate to the cited article.
